name: Multivariate Analysis Conventions
description: This module defines the naming, formatting, and structural style conventions to follow whenever writing, implementing, or reviewing multivariate analysis code or output, so results stay consistent with the existing multivariate analysis style guide.
content:
This module defines the naming, formatting, and structural style conventions to follow whenever writing, implementing, or reviewing multivariate analysis code or output, so results stay consistent with the existing multivariate analysis style guide.

CORE GUIDELINES
1. Validate multivariate analysis outputs against a concrete example before treating the work as complete.
2. When multivariate analysis guidance conflicts with a specific user instruction, defer to the user's explicit instruction and note the conflict.
3. Measure before optimizing any multivariate analysis bottleneck; do not guess at what is slow.
4. When multivariate analysis decisions are ambiguous, favor the option that is easiest to reverse or extend later.
5. Prefer explicit, readable multivariate analysis solutions over clever ones that are hard to verify.
6. When multiple multivariate analysis strategies are viable, name the trade-off explicitly rather than silently picking one.
7. Keep multivariate analysis changes scoped to what was asked; avoid unrelated cleanup in the same pass.
8. Re-check edge cases relevant to multivariate analysis (empty input, boundary values, concurrent access) before calling the task done.
9. Document any non-obvious multivariate analysis decision with a short rationale so future readers understand the 'why', not just the 'what'.
10. Check that multivariate analysis terminology is used consistently throughout, matching existing conventions in the surrounding context.
11. Surface known limitations of a chosen multivariate analysis approach instead of presenting it as complete when it is not.
12. Prefer the simplest multivariate analysis approach that satisfies the requirement over a more general one that isn't needed yet.

COMMON PITFALLS TO AVOID
- Avoid mixing unrelated multivariate analysis concerns into a single change; keep each change focused.
- Do not treat a single passing example as full verification of multivariate analysis correctness.
- Avoid introducing new multivariate analysis abstractions before there is a second concrete use case that needs them.

CLOSING NOTE
These guidelines are a starting point for multivariate analysis, not an exhaustive rulebook — use judgment when a rule doesn't fit the situation.
